text: You've spent two courses building identity architecture and dual-cloud security controls. This chapter is where those pieces get a name for the model they're actually serving: Zero Trust. Before the tenets and the architecture, start with the failure that made Zero Trust necessary in the first place — why the old perimeter model, the one built around firewalls and VPNs, stopped being able to protect what enterprises actually run today.

Castle-and-moat security assumed three things that used to be reasonable. The enterprise owned its network infrastructure end to end. Devices on that network were enterprise-managed and inventoried. And users proved trust once, at login or VPN connection, and that trust was treated as ongoing for as long as they stayed on the network. Under those conditions, network location was a genuinely useful stand-in for trust.

Four real shifts broke those assumptions. Cloud and SaaS moved your most sensitive resources outside any network you own. Remote and hybrid work flipped the default user location from inside the office to outside it, over the open internet. BYOD and third parties needed access without ever fitting the managed-device assumption. And lateral movement is the one that breaks the security promise itself — once an attacker is inside, implicit trust lets them move sideways with almost no resistance.

Stated plainly, the perimeter model equated network location with trust: inside the firewall meant trusted, outside meant untrusted. NIST SP 800-207 starts from the opposite premise — that an enterprise's resources, users, and devices no longer sit inside one boundary, so a model that trusts based on location can no longer protect them. That's not a case against firewalls or VPNs. It's a case against treating location as proof of trust.

Keep your VPNs, your NSGs, your firewall rules — you'll still use all of them. What changes is what they're allowed to decide on their own. Next lesson walks through the seven tenets NIST SP 800-207 proposes to replace location-based trust: resources, secured communication, per-session access, dynamic policy, continuous monitoring, strict enforcement, and the telemetry loop that keeps improving all of it.
